title: J&K braces for week-long wet spell; IMD warns of heavy rain in Jammu - thekashmirimages.com
article_text:
SRINAGAR: Jammu and Kashmir is likely to witness a fresh spell of rain and thunderstorms over the next week, with the India Meteorological Department (IMD) forecasting widespread precipitation and warning of flash floods, landslides and mudslides in vulnerable areas.
According to the Meteorological Centre, Srinagar, Kashmir is expected to receive fairly widespread light to moderate rainfall from August 17 to 20, followed by scattered showers on August 21 and 22. Jammu division is likely to witness widespread rainfall during August 17–20, with the intensity reducing to fairly widespread activity over the subsequent two days.
The weather office has forecast isolated thunder, lightning and gusty winds of 30–40 kmph across Kashmir during the seven-day period and warned of landslides, mudslides, shooting stones and flash floods at vulnerable locations.
Jammu division is expected to experience a more intense spell, with isolated heavy to very heavy rainfall forecast between August 16 and 20. Thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds of up to 40 kmph are also likely during the period. Similar warnings for landslides, mudslides, shooting stones and flash floods remain in place.
For August 21 and 22, isolated thunder and lightning accompanied by gusty winds are expected to continue in Jammu division.
On Monday, Srinagar is likely to witness partly cloudy skies with light rain or thunderstorms. The maximum and minimum temperatures are expected to hover around 29°C and 21°C, respectively.
Jammu city is forecast to remain generally cloudy with moderate to heavy rain or thunderstorms, with temperatures around 32°C and 27°C. Muzaffarabad and Mirpur are also expected to receive light to moderate rain or thunderstorms, with maximum temperatures of around 34°C and 33°C, respectively.
During the past 24 hours ending at 8:30 am on Sunday, maximum temperatures across Kashmir remained 0–3°C above normal, while temperatures in Jammu division were generally 0–2°C above normal.
Srinagar recorded the highest daytime temperature in Kashmir at 32°C, while Kathua was the warmest place in Jammu division at 32.8°C.
Night temperatures remained around normal in most parts of Kashmir and up to 3°C above normal at several places in Jammu division. Gulmarg recorded the lowest minimum temperature in Kashmir at 11.6°C, while Bhaderwah recorded 17.4°C in Jammu.
The weather office said light to moderate rainfall was recorded at several places during the period, with Jammu receiving the highest rainfall of 4.9 mm. The station chart also recorded 41 mm rainfall in Mirpur.
The IMD has advised residents, particularly those living in vulnerable areas, to remain alert as the wet spell could trigger flash floods, landslides, mudslides and shooting stones in susceptible locations.
The forecast is valid from August 16 to August 23.

title: Mumbai Rain Alert Today: IMD has Predicted Rainfall in Mumbai, Thane, and Several Parts of Maharashtra - NativePlanet
article_text:
Maharashtra is likely to experience another spell of monsoon rain, with several districts expected to receive moderate to heavy showers. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has warned of heavy rainfall at isolated places, particularly in parts of the Konkan region. Raigad, Ratnagiri and Sindhudurg are among the areas that need to remain cautious.
Mumbai and Thane are also expected to receive rain today. The IMD forecast indicates light to moderate rainfall in Mumbai, while Thane may see moderate showers. Rain is likely to continue over the next few days, although the intensity may vary.
Raigad is expected to receive moderate rainfall, with heavy showers possible at isolated locations. Ratnagiri and Sindhudurg may also experience heavy rainfall in some areas. The weather department has advised people in vulnerable locations to remain alert, especially because heavy rain can increase the risk of waterlogging, flooding and landslides.
Nashik is likely to see light rain and thunderstorms, while the surrounding Ghats may receive moderate showers. Pune and Satara are expected to have light rainfall, but heavy rain remains possible in the Ghat areas of both districts. Sangli is likely to receive light rain.
The IMD has also warned of problems caused by heavy rain, including waterlogging in low-lying areas, flash floods, falling trees, damage to weak structures and disruption to road, rail, air and ferry services. Coastal areas may experience rough sea conditions and strong winds. Landslides and mudslides are also possible in vulnerable hilly regions.
People are advised to check weather and traffic updates before travelling and avoid open areas during thunderstorms. Residents should also stay away from tall trees, water bodies and weak structures during periods of heavy rain or lightning. The IMD has urged people to follow local authorities' advisories and regularly check updated forecasts as monsoon conditions can change quickly.

Monsoon: Heavy rain warnings in Punjab, Bihar, Himachal, Gujarat

09:49 am
What's the story

The monsoon has become irregular across India, with the rain-bearing trough moving away from Delhi-NCR and easing over Maharashtra. However, heavy rains are expected in Punjab, Bihar, Himachal Pradesh, and Gujarat.
Mumbai and Thane experienced intermittent rain on Monday morning.
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has issued alerts for thunderstorms and locally heavy rainfall in several states throughout the day.


Forecast discrepancies

Delhi's weather forecast today

There is a difference in reports regarding Delhi's weather.

Live Hindustan reports that the monsoon axis has shifted toward the Himalayan foothills, reducing activity over Delhi-NCR. The report rules out heavy rain for the next few days, predicting light cloud cover and isolated drizzle instead.

However, The Economic Times cites IMD as forecasting heavy rain and thunderstorms in Delhi today with a high of nearly 34°C and low of nearly 28°C.

title: Jharkhand Weather : 14 जिलों में भारी बारिश का अलर्ट, आंधी-तूफान के भी आसार - lagatar.in
article_text:
Ranchi News : झारखंड में मॉनसून एक बार फिर जोर पकड़ता नजर आ रहा है. सोमवार को राज्य के कई हिस्सों में बारिश और बादल छाए रहने की संभावना है. मौसम विभाग ने 17 और 18 अगस्त को कई जिलों में भारी बारिश को लेकर चेतावनी जारी की है.

मौसम विभाग के अनुसार, खूंटी, रांची, पूर्वी सिंहभूम, पश्चिमी सिंहभूम, सरायकेला-खरसावां, रामगढ़, हजारीबाग, गिरिडीह, दुमका, लातेहार, गुमला, सिमडेगा, लोहरदगा और चतरा में भारी बारिश के साथ आंधी-तूफान की स्थिति बन सकती है.

इस दौरान 50 किलोमीटर प्रति घंटे की रफ्तार से हवाएं चल सकती है. झारखंड की खबरें पढ़ने के लिए यहां क्लिक करें...

कई जिलों में मौसम रहेगा सुहावना

बारिश और बादलों के कारण रांची, खूंटी, गुमला, सिमडेगा, पश्चिमी सिंहभूम और सरायकेला-खरसावां में तापमान में राहत मिल सकती है. इन इलाकों में मौसम अपेक्षाकृत सुहावना रहने की उम्मीद है.

19 अगस्त के बाद राहत, पर पूरी तरह नहीं थमेगी बारिश

मौसम विभाग के अनुसार, 18 और 19 अगस्त के बाद बारिश की तीव्रता में कुछ कमी आ सकती है. इसके बावजूद कई इलाकों में गरज के साथ बारिश जारी रहेगी. 20 अगस्त को कुछ जगहों पर हल्की या छिटपुट बारिश हो सकती है.

रांची-देवघर सहित कई शहरों में आंधी-बारिश के आसार

वहीं 21 अगस्त तक राज्य में बारिश का असर बने रहने की संभावना है. आईएमडी के अनुसार, रांची, जमशेदपुर, धनबाद, बोकारो, दुमका, हजारीबाग, पलामू, रामगढ़, खूंटी, सिमडेगा और देवघर में भी बारिश के साथ तेज हवा और वज्रपात की संभावना जताई गई है.

लोगों को सतर्क रहने की दी सलाह

मौसम विभाग ने खराब मौसम में लोगों को सतर्क रहने की सलाह दी है. इस दौरान जरूरी काम नहीं होने पर घर से बाहर नहीं निकलने की सलाह दी है. साथ ही बिजली चमकने परखुले मैदान, पेड़, बिजली के खंभों और अन्य असुरक्षित स्थानों से दूर रहने को कहा है.

title: Rescue must begin before the disaster: Inside NDRF’s pre-monsoon strategy in Kerala - Deccan Herald
article_text:
At 6 am on July 31, my phone began to buzz. The calls were about an unfolding operation in Kerala, and what followed was a reminder of a simple truth: the most successful rescue is often the one that begins before the disaster does.
Experience a more refined e-paper today
By the time the heavy rain set in, over the first five days of August, the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) personnel were already on the ground. As part of the pre-monsoon preparedness mechanism, 11 teams (a full NDRF team is 47 personnel) had been pre-positioned across the state ahead of it. Their deployment was not a reaction to a disaster that had already happened; it was a response to the possibility of one.
The decisive work of disaster management happens largely unseen, well before the first rescue call is made — in forecasting, the pre-positioning of resources, evacuation planning and coordination.
A rainfall figure, on its own, rarely tells the whole story. When the heavy rain arrived, it had to be read together with the state of the reservoirs, because rain running into catchments that are already brimming behaves very differently from the same rain on empty ground.
The dam bulletin reaching the state emergency operations centre tells its own story: in Idukki, Lower Periyar is at its full reservoir level, Kallarkutty has crossed 96%, and several major reservoirs remain in the red, still spilling water through their gates more than a week after the downpour.
With the dams this full, even the light-to-moderate rain is not a small matter. It is the two readings together, rainfall and reservoir level, that show where the danger lies. Kautilya understood this 2000 years ago: his Arthashastra speaks of preparing the counter to an adversity before it arrives, vinipāta-pratīkāra. Do not wait for the crisis to prepare for it.
The clearest lesson of the operation was the value of having specialised forces already in place. The NDRF teams were positioned in advance, with the State Disaster Response Force, Fire and Rescue Services and Civil Defence volunteers ready to reinforce them.
Many of those volunteers had come through NDRF training programmes run across several states in the preceding months, and the Kerala State Disaster Management Authority had run multi-agency tabletop exercises before the monsoon so that when the calls came, most of those in the room had, in effect, already rehearsed the day once.
All of this buys the thing that matters most in a flood: time. When a settlement is cut off, the difference between a team already in the district and one still being moved from far away is measured in lives. The point is not more personnel on paper, but the right people and expertise in the right place before conditions turn.
Rescue makes the news, but it is the wrong yardstick. The better measure is how many people never had to be rescued at all, because they were moved out in time. Through those five days of heavy rain, more than 3,000 people were evacuated to safety in coordinated moves involving the the NDRF, the SDRF, Civil Defence and the district administration. A reactive system counts the people it has to pull out of danger; an anticipatory one counts the people it can move to safety before the danger reaches them. The second count is the one that should define the work.
No single agency handles a major disaster on its own. This response held because the district administration, the NDRF, the SDRF, Fire and Rescue Services, Civil Defence and the meteorological and dam-monitoring agencies were working on the same page. At its best, coordination of this kind becomes something more deliberate: fusion.
In the older model, uniformed forces are called in only after local capacity is already overwhelmed; civil–military fusion turns that around. It has the civil administration and the uniformed forces, the NDRF, the state forces, and, in larger emergencies, the armed forces, planning together and operating as one system from the first hour, rather than as separate columns that meet for the first time in the middle of a crisis. That integration cannot be assembled once the water is rising. It has to be built earlier, in agreed command arrangements, standing liaison and joint rehearsals. Kerala’s pre-monsoon deployment, cross-state training and tabletop drills were exactly this groundwork.
Incidents like this one should not stay as isolated lessons. They should shape a broader disaster-management doctrine built on four plain steps: forecast, prepare, pre-position and evacuate, held together by fusion between civilian and uniformed responders. Technology helps at every step, from real-time reservoir data to interoperable communications, but technology alone does not save lives; institutional preparedness, and the willingness to act on it, do.
The writer is an assistant commandant, National Disaster Response Force.

title: 17-18 अगस्त को मौसम का बड़ा अलर्ट! हरियाणा-पंजाब से हिमाचल तक भारी बारिश, कई इलाकों में बाढ़ का खतरा - Amrit Vichar
article_text:
17-18 अगस्त को मौसम का बड़ा अलर्ट! हरियाणा-पंजाब से हिमाचल तक भारी बारिश, कई इलाकों में बाढ़ का खतरा
Amrit Vichar Network
By Muskan Dixit
Edited By Muskan Dixit
On 17 Aug 2026 10:32:50
उत्तर भारत में फिर सक्रिय हुआ बारिश का दौर
IMD ने हरियाणा, पंजाब, चंडीगढ़ और दिल्ली में 17-18 अगस्त को भारी बारिश की संभावना जताई है। हिमाचल प्रदेश और जम्मू-कश्मीर-लद्दाख में बहुत भारी बारिश का अनुमान है। उत्तराखंड और पहाड़ी इलाकों के कुछ जलग्रहण क्षेत्रों में अचानक बाढ़ का कम से मध्यम जोखिम भी बताया गया है।

डिजिटल डेस्कः उत्तर भारत के कई राज्यों में अगले कुछ दिनों तक मौसम का मिजाज बिगड़ा रह सकता है। भारत मौसम विज्ञान विभाग (IMD) के अनुसार, हरियाणा, चंडीगढ़, दिल्ली और पंजाब में 17 और 18 अगस्त को अलग-अलग स्थानों पर भारी बारिश होने की संभावना है। 18 अगस्त को इन क्षेत्रों में बारिश का दायरा बढ़ सकता है और अधिकांश स्थानों पर बारिश होने का अनुमान है।

पश्चिमी हिमालयी क्षेत्र में बारिश की तीव्रता इससे अधिक रहने की आशंका है। हिमाचल प्रदेश में 17 और 18 अगस्त को कुछ स्थानों पर बहुत भारी बारिश हो सकती है। जम्मू-कश्मीर, लद्दाख, गिलगित-बाल्टिस्तान और मुजफ्फराबाद में 17 से 19 अगस्त तक बहुत भारी बारिश की संभावना जताई गई है।

हिमाचल से उत्तराखंड तक भारी बारिश की चेतावनी

17 अगस्त को हिमाचल प्रदेश, जम्मू-कश्मीर-लद्दाख-गिलगित-बाल्टिस्तान-मुजफ्फराबाद और उत्तराखंड में अलग-अलग स्थानों पर भारी से बहुत भारी बारिश हो सकती है। उत्तर प्रदेश, अरुणाचल प्रदेश, छत्तीसगढ़, पूर्वी मध्य प्रदेश, गांगेय पश्चिम बंगाल और झारखंड में भी कुछ स्थानों पर भारी से बहुत भारी बारिश का पूर्वानुमान है।

18 अगस्त को हिमाचल प्रदेश, जम्मू-कश्मीर-लद्दाख-गिलगित-बाल्टिस्तान-मुजफ्फराबाद और पूर्वी उत्तर प्रदेश में भारी से बहुत भारी बारिश की संभावना है। वहीं अरुणाचल प्रदेश, झारखंड तथा पश्चिम बंगाल और सिक्किम के कुछ हिस्सों में भी तेज बारिश हो सकती है।

हरियाणा, चंडीगढ़, दिल्ली, पंजाब, उत्तराखंड और पश्चिमी उत्तर प्रदेश में 18 अगस्त को अलग-अलग स्थानों पर भारी बारिश का अनुमान है।

23 अगस्त तक पहाड़ों में बना रहेगा बारिश का असर

आईएमडी के अनुसार पश्चिमी हिमालयी क्षेत्र में पूरे सप्ताह बारिश का दौर जारी रह सकता है। हिमाचल प्रदेश, जम्मू-कश्मीर-लद्दाख-गिलगित-बाल्टिस्तान-मुजफ्फराबाद और उत्तराखंड में 17 से 23 अगस्त तक अधिकांश स्थानों पर बारिश होने का अनुमान है।

हिमाचल प्रदेश में 17-18 अगस्त की बहुत भारी बारिश के बाद 19 से 23 अगस्त तक भी कुछ स्थानों पर भारी बारिश जारी रह सकती है। उत्तराखंड में 18 से 23 अगस्त तक भारी बारिश की संभावना है।

19 अगस्त को हिमाचल प्रदेश और उत्तराखंड में भारी बारिश हो सकती है, जबकि जम्मू-कश्मीर-लद्दाख-गिलगित-बाल्टिस्तान-मुजफ्फराबाद में कुछ स्थानों पर भारी से बहुत भारी बारिश का अनुमान है। हिमाचल प्रदेश और उत्तराखंड में 20 और 21 अगस्त तथा 22 और 23 अगस्त को भी कुछ इलाकों में भारी बारिश जारी रह सकती है।

अचानक बाढ़ का भी खतरा, इन इलाकों पर नजर

आईएमडी ने 18 अगस्त सुबह 5:30 बजे तक के लिए 24 घंटे का फ्लैश फ्लड रिस्क फोरकास्ट भी जारी किया है। इसके मुताबिक हिमाचल प्रदेश, जम्मू-कश्मीर-लद्दाख और उत्तराखंड के कुछ जलग्रहण क्षेत्रों तथा आसपास के इलाकों में अचानक बाढ़ का कम से मध्यम खतरा है।

हिमाचल प्रदेश: चंबा, कांगड़ा, मंडी, शिमला और सिरमौर के कुछ इलाके।

जम्मू-कश्मीर और लद्दाख: डोडा, कठुआ, उधमपुर और लद्दाख का लेह क्षेत्र।

उत्तराखंड: बागेश्वर, चमोली, चंपावत, देहरादून, पौड़ी गढ़वाल, टिहरी गढ़वाल, नैनीताल, पिथौरागढ़, रुद्रप्रयाग और उत्तरकाशी के कुछ क्षेत्र।

आईएमडी के मुताबिक संभावित बारिश के कारण पहले से संतृप्त मिट्टी वाले क्षेत्रों और निचले इलाकों में सतही पानी का बहाव बढ़ने या जलभराव की स्थिति बन सकती है।

आखिर क्यों बिगड़ा मौसम? कई सिस्टम सक्रिय

मौसम में बदलाव के पीछे एक से अधिक मौसमी प्रणालियां सक्रिय हैं। आईएमडी के 17 अगस्त सुबह 5:30 बजे के विश्लेषण के अनुसार, उत्तर-पश्चिम बंगाल की खाड़ी और उससे सटे पश्चिम बंगाल-उत्तरी ओडिशा तट पर बना निम्न दबाव क्षेत्र उत्तर-पश्चिम की ओर बढ़कर अवदाब (Depression) में बदल गया है।

सुबह 5:30 बजे यह अवदाब तटीय पश्चिम बंगाल, उससे सटे बांग्लादेश और उत्तर-पश्चिम बंगाल की खाड़ी के ऊपर कोलकाता के निकट केंद्रित था। आईएमडी के अनुसार, इसके अगले 24 घंटों में गांगेय पश्चिम बंगाल से होते हुए उत्तर-पश्चिम दिशा में झारखंड की ओर बढ़ने की प्रबल संभावना है।

इसके अलावा समुद्र तल पर मानसून की द्रोणिका फिरोजपुर, देहरादून, बरेली, सुल्तानपुर, डाल्टनगंज और जमशेदपुर से गुजरते हुए अवदाब के केंद्र तक बनी हुई थी। यह प्रणाली आगे दक्षिण-पूर्व दिशा में उत्तर-पूर्व बंगाल की खाड़ी तक फैली थी।

उत्तर-पश्चिम उत्तर प्रदेश के ऊपर समुद्र तल से 0.9 किलोमीटर की ऊंचाई पर ऊपरी हवा का चक्रवाती परिसंचरण बना हुआ है। जम्मू संभाग और आसपास के क्षेत्रों में भी समुद्र तल से 5.8 किलोमीटर की ऊंचाई पर ऊपरी हवा का चक्रवाती परिसंचरण मौजूद है।

पंजाब और उत्तराखंड में कई जगह हुई बारिश

आईएमडी के अनुसार 16 अगस्त सुबह 8:30 बजे से 17 अगस्त सुबह 5:30 बजे तक पंजाब और उत्तराखंड में अधिकांश स्थानों पर बारिश दर्ज की गई। जम्मू-कश्मीर और लद्दाख में भी कई स्थानों पर बारिश हुई।

मौसम विभाग ने यह भी स्पष्ट किया है कि चेतावनी में इस्तेमाल किया गया लाल रंग 'रेड अलर्ट' का अर्थ नहीं रखता, बल्कि इसका मतलब 'कार्रवाई करें' है।

आईएमडी के अनुसार किसी भी दिन का मौसम पूर्वानुमान और चेतावनी उस दिन सुबह 8:30 बजे से अगले दिन सुबह 8:30 बजे तक प्रभावी रहती है।

title: Waterlogging Exposes Dimapur Airport’s Location Limits; State Must Plan New Infra - Nagaland Post
article_text:
Staff Reporter

DIMAPUR, AUG 16 (NPN): The repeated waterlogging of the runway at Dimapur Airport should no longer be treated as a seasonal inconvenience or an isolated operational problem. It is a warning that the airport is facing a deeper ecological and infrastructure crisis that cannot be solved through repeated short term repairs.

Despite interventions by the Airports Authority of India (AAI) and the state Water Resources department, flooding continues to disrupt airport operations during heavy monsoon spells. The recurrence of the problem raises a larger question: can the existing site realistically meet Nagaland’s future aviation needs?

The fundamental problem is not simply the airport’s ageing infrastructure but the location and topography of the site.

Situated in a low lying area close to the Chathe River and surrounded by drainage constraints, the airport is particularly vulnerable to waterlogging. Its proximity to the nearby Hills also creates limitations for runway alignment and future expansion.

Water from areas around the former Sugar Mill village and the North East Zone Cultural Centre (NEZCC) flows towards the airport. The situation is made worse by an inadequate urban drainage system, with several local nullahs blocked by garbage, encroachment and restricted water flow.

The raised embankment of National Highway 29 is another major concern. Instead of allowing water to follow its natural course, the highway embankment obstructs the flow and contributes to water collecting around the airport.

During intense rainfall, the consequences become severe. When water on the runway rises to around 60 millimetres against an operational safety threshold of about 3 millimetres, flights have to be cancelled. This is not simply an airport management issue. It points to a larger problem with the location and surrounding infrastructure.

The airport also faces serious physical limitations. Residential structures and a cemetery are located close to the security perimeter, leaving little room for meaningful expansion or the creation of adequate buffer areas. The existing runway, measuring about 7,513 feet in length and 147 feet in width, is also limited when viewed against the requirements of modern aviation.

If Nagaland wants Dimapur to function as a major regional or international gateway, the state will eventually need a substantially longer and wider runway, potentially in the range of 8,000 to 9,000 feet in length and up to 200 feet in width. Such expansion, however, cannot be considered in isolation from the surrounding terrain.

Dimapur Airport currently handles roughly 3.37 lakh passengers a year, or about 900 passenger movements a day, making reliable and future-ready air connectivity a necessity rather than a luxury for Nagaland.

Recent AAI-reported data shows that on August 9, 2026, Dimapur handled three arrivals and three departures, or six scheduled movements, with 1,102 passengers.

This limited capacity should not be mistaken for limited demand. Rather, it demonstrates the need to plan ahead for an airport capable of handling substantially greater passenger and aircraft traffic as Nagaland’s economy, tourism and business activity expand

In order to expand the airport with modern facilities etc, land is needed.

The Assam Rifles has handed over 18.8 acres to AAI for Phase I of the Dimapur Airport expansion. The remaining roughly around 129 acres is to be transferred for Phase II, subject to approval from the competent authorities.

The other aspect of the Dimapur Airport is its constraint by hilly terrain on several sides, particularly toward the south-east, north-east and north-west.

The terrain is especially significant on the Runway 30 side, which has contributed to the airport’s largely unidirectional operation, with aircraft landing from the Runway 12 end

According to an official source, a recent court record concerning the airport expansion states that the airport is presently operated essentially as a unidirectional runway because of the hilly terrain on the Runway 30 side. It says aircraft land from the Runway 12 end.

A south west to north east alignment could provide a more suitable flight corridor by keeping the hills largely to the sides rather than directly along the aircraft approach and departure paths. But achieving such an alignment at the existing site would require land, space and terrain conditions that are extremely difficult to secure.

This is why the debate should move beyond another round of drainage works and temporary flood control measures. The fundamental question is whether it is worth continuing to invest in an airport whose geography places a permanent limit on its expansion and operational reliability.

A new airport at Chümoukedima deserves serious and immediate consideration. The area offers greater scope for planning a modern airport from the beginning, including a longer runway, safer alignment, better drainage, adequate safety zones and room for future expansion.

A properly planned airport could become more than a replacement for Dimapur Airport. It could become the foundation of Nagaland’s future economic connectivity.

The urgency is greater because neighbouring Assam is also expanding its aviation ambitions. A proposed airport at Chotalangfer, or Borlangphar, under the Diphu revenue circle, could eventually provide direct air links to major cities such as Kolkata, Delhi, Bengaluru, Chennai and Mumbai. The proposed site is only about 45 kilometres from Nagaland’s border with Assam, making the competition for regional connectivity real.

Nagaland therefore cannot afford to remain trapped in a cycle of repairing the old while postponing decisions about the future. Every major disruption at Dimapur Airport should be seen as a reminder of what is at stake.

Air connectivity is no longer a luxury. It is central to tourism, business, investment, education, health services and regional economic growth. If Nagaland wants to build a modern economy, it needs modern infrastructure to support it.

The state government must therefore begin a serious technical and feasibility assessment for an alternative airport at Chümoukedima and make the findings public. The issue should not be reduced to another political announcement or a seasonal response to flooding. Nagaland needs a long term aviation plan.

If Dimapur Airport has reached the limits imposed by its geography, the answer is not to keep fighting the geography. The answer is to plan a better location. Otherwise, the state’s ambitious economic plans may remain disconnected from the very infrastructure needed to make them possible.
